L146: Our analysis reveals that the dissimilarity between harmful and safe inputs progressively rises mostly in the middle layers and reaches the peak at middle-to-late layers (c.f. Figure cite100†2 ). It indicates that safety mechanisms are most prevalent in middle-to-late regions. We compute the first-order differences in the average cosine dissimilarity between harmful and safe representations across layers to identify the boundaries where these differences are most pronounced.
L147: Specifically, we evaluate the change in cosine distance between successive layers with a threshold, $\tau$^{5}^{5} 5 The value of $\tau$ is set to $0.04$ to select the boundary indices i.e. $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$. The full procedure is detailed in Algorithm cite101†1 .

L182: Next, we find the optimal scaling factor, denoted as $\lambda^{*}$ that maximizes the impact while preserving general language modeling capabilities. To ensure the balance, we employ Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to quantify the discrepancy between output distributions with and without SABER (c.f. Algorithm cite102†2 ). The algorithm iterates over a predefined set of candidate $\lambda$ values, $\Lambda$.
L183: For each value of $\lambda$, we compute the average distributional difference between the output of the original model, $\mathcal{M}_{\theta}$ and the modified model, $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$. Here, $\pi^{x}_{\text{orig}}$ and $\pi^{x}_{s,e,\lambda}$ represents the probability distribution over the final token of $x$ from $\mathcal{M}_{\theta}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$, respectively.
L184: Note that $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$ is modified with a residual connection from layer $s$ to layer $e$ scaled by a factor of $\lambda$. For each instance in $\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}^{\text{ val}}$, a pair of layer $(s,e)$ is randomly selected within valid boundaries i.e. $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$ to incorporate the residual connection.
L185: The algorithm accumulates the average KL divergence for each $\lambda$ over $\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}^{\text{ val}}$ but retains only those values in $\lambda^{*}_{list}$ if the divergence remains below a threshold of $\psi$^{6}^{6} 6 The value of $\psi$ is set to $0.05$. It ensures minimal impact of SABER on the model’s general performance for benign inputs while maximizing the impact on harmful prompts. Finally, it returns the maximum value from $\lambda^{*}_{list}$.
L186: Additional information on the sensitivity of $\lambda$ is given in Appendix cite38†A.4 .

L217: #### 4.2.3 Identification of the Optimal Pair
L218: Now, we identify the pair of optimal layers, denoted as $(s^{*},e^{*})$ within the range defined by $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$ (c.f. Algorithm cite103†3 ). It considers all possible pairs of layers $(i,j)$ where $i<j$ and an altered model $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,i,j}$ with a residual connection from layer $i$ to layer $j$.
L219: The altered model $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,i,j}$ is evaluated on the $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{val}}$ validation set, yielding a success rate using the HarmBench metric defined in Section cite19†5.4 . Finally, the pair $(i,j)$ with the highest success rate is returned as the optimal configuration $(s^{*},e^{*})$. We evaluate all possible pairs within the identified boundaries to pinpoint the optimal pair $(s^{*},e^{*})$ that yields highest success rate on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$.
L220: Additional information regarding the optimal value for each of the parameters are given in Appendix cite37†A.3 .
L221: ## 5 Experimental Setup
L222: 
L223: ### 5.1 Models
L224: 
L225: We integrate SABER with four alternative models: (i) Llama-2-7b-chat^{7}^{7} 7 cite104†https://huggingface.co/meta-llama†huggingface.co (L2-7BCh) (ii) Llama-2-13b-chat (L2-13BCh) (iii) Vicuna-7b-v1.5^{8}^{8} 8 cite105†https://huggingface.co/lmsys†huggingface.co (V-7B) and (iv) Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2^{9}^{9} 9 cite106†https://huggingface.co/mistralai†huggingface.co (M-7BInst).
L226: ### 5.2 Benchmark Datasets
L227: We benchmark SABER against the baselines (c.f. Section cite18†5.3 ) and its architectural variants (c.f. Section cite20†5.5 ) on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ test}}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$ of the HarmBench dataset, respectively . To further validate the effectiveness of SABER under more stringent scenario, we leverage $520$ instances from AdvBench cite107†Biarese (2022) and $100$ instances from JailbreakBench (JbBench) cite108†Chao et al. (2024) .
L228: Moreover, we report whether SABER negatively affects the general capabilities of the models or not through assessing the models (c.f. Section cite16†5.1 ) based on the coherence of generated outputs and their performance in reasoning tasks, both with and without SABER on widely recognized benchmarks: MMLU cite109†Hendrycks et al. (2020) , TinyHellaSwag cite110†Zellers et al. (2019) , ARC cite111†Clark et al. (2018) , WinoGrande cite112†Sakaguchi et al. (2021) and TruthfulQA cite113†Lin et al. (2021) .
L229: Additional information on the evaluation prompts is presented in Appendix cite42†B .
L230: ### 5.3 Baseline
L231: We use the following baselines against SABER: (i) GCG cite70†Zou et al. (2023b) , (ii) GCG-M, (iii) GCG-T, (iv) AutoPrompt cite114†Shin et al. (2020) , (v) PAIR cite115†Chao et al. (2023) and (vii) AutoDAN cite116†Liu et al. (2023) . GCG is a token-level method that optimizes an adversarial suffix to increase the likelihood of an inappropriate target string.
L232: It has two variants: (i) GCG-M that optimizes a single adversarial suffix to be appended with multiple user prompts, each targeting a different target string; and (ii) GCG-T that builds upon GCG-M by simultaneously optimizing the adversarial suffix across multiple training models. AutoPrompt is similar to GCG, but it uses a different strategy for selection of candidate prompts. PAIR opts for iterative prompting strategy to explore and adaptively obtain harmful responses.
L233: Lastly, AutoDan uses a hierarchical genetic algorithm to alter the handcrafted adversarial prompts inorder to generate inappropriate responses.
L234: ### 5.4 Evaluation Metric
L235: We adopt A ttack S uccess R ate (ASR) as an evaluation metric for successful jailbreaks following the default framework employed in HarmBench and JbBench. The target model $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$ generates^{10}^{10} 10 Following the default setup, we use greedy decoding to generate $512$ new tokens for HarmBench and $150$ for JbBench. a sequence of output tokens, $\hat{x}$, conditioned on the given test input $x$ i.e. $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}(x)=\hat{x}$.
L236: Thereafter, a classification model ($\mathcal{M}_{\phi}$) is leveraged to assign a binary label to each output sequence where the label of $1$ indicates $success$ and $0$ indicates $failure$. ASR is defined as the proportion of success over the total number of test instances.
L237:  | $$\text{ASR}=\frac{1}{|D_{harm}^{test}|}\sum_{x\in D_{harm}^{test}}\mathcal{M}_{\phi}(\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}(x))$$  |
L238: HarmBench uses a fine-tuned Mistral-7B-v0.1 (HB-ValCls) model for validation and a fine-tuned Llama-2-13b-chat model (HB-TestCls) for test evaluation. In contrast, JbBench prompts a pre-trained Llama-3-70B-Instruct (JB-TestCls) for overall evaluation. In our work, we utilize the validation classifier of HarmBench to validate the intra-variants performances but leverage the test classifier to assess SABER against the baselines.
L239: We use perplexity^{11}^{11} 11 First $64$ new tokens are consider and evaluated based on the probabilities of Llama-2-13b. and ASR^{12}^{12} 12 First $512$ new tokens are considered and evaluated using HB-ValCls. to analyze the different variants of SABER. Note that in the absence of any default evaluation setting, we utilize the evaluation setting from JbBench for AdvBench.
L240: Moreover, we use ROUGE cite117†Lin (2004) score for TruthfulQA and accuracy for other datasets to assess the impact of SABER on reasoning ability.
L241: ### 5.5 Variations of SABER
L242: This section outlines five distinct variations of SABER. The first variation Org, retains the original architecture of the underlying model. The second variation is SABER, normalizes $\tilde{h}_{i}^{(s)}$ with its Euclidean norm and scales it up by the Euclidean norm of $h_{i}^{(e)}$. In contrast, the third variation NoENorm, excludes Euclidean norm for $\tilde{h}_{i}^{(s)}$.
L243: The fourth variation, referred as NoLNorm, excludes the use of layer normalization for $h_{i}^{(s)}$ but uses Euclidean norm of $h_{i}^{(s)}$. Lastly, the fifth variation, denoted as IntP, uses both the layer normalization and Euclidean norm. In addition, IntP interpolates between the original stream and residual connection. Additional information for each variation is provided in Appendix cite43†C .

L262: ## 6 Results
L263: This section presents the performance of SABER for each of the following models: L2-7BCh, L2-13BCh, V-7B and M-7BInstV2 with two distinct variants: (i) one that excludes the default system prompts ($\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$) (c.f. Appendix cite35†A.1 ) and (ii) the other one ($\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$) that includes it (c.f. Appendix cite36†A.2 ).
L264: We report results with and without system prompts, as benchmarks typically use default prompts for evaluation, which is less relevant for white-box attacks where the attackers can easily exclude these prompts. We use the test set $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ test}}$ from HarmBench to compare SABER with the baselines (see Table cite118†1 ), and the test sets from AdvBench and JbBench to further demonstrate the efficiency of SABER (see Table cite119†2 ).
L265: ### 6.1 Benchmarking Against Baselines
L266: Table cite118†1 shows that the baseline GCG scores highest among the baselines although AutoDAN exceeds GCG in case of M-7BInstV2.
L267: While GCG scores $34.5$, $28.0$, $90.0$ and $88.0$ for L2-7BCh, L2-13BCh, V-7B and M-7BInstV2, respectively, the closest-performing baselines are GCG-M for L2-7BCh with a score of $20.0$ (a gap of $14.5\%$), PAIR for L2-13BCh with a score of $15.0$ (trailing by $13.0\%$), AutoDAN for V-7B with a score of $89.5$ (with a deficit of $0.5\%$) and AutoDAN for M-7BInstV2 with a score of $93$ ahead of GCG by $5\%$. Note that for M-7BInstV2, AutoDAN outperforms GCG.
L268: $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ performs better than all the baselines in all scenarios. $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ scores $85.5$ for L2-7BCh, outperforming GCG by $51\%$, $66.7$ for L2-13BCh ahead of GCG by $38.7\%$, $93.1$ for V-7B surpassing GCG and AutoDan by $3.1\%$ and $3.6\%$, respectively. In case of M-7BInstV2, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ achieves $93.1$, yielding a gain of $0.1\%$ and $5.1\%$ over AutoDAN and GCG, respectively.
L269: ### 6.2 Benchmarking Against JbBench and AdvBench
L270: We further assess SABER on the JbBench and AdvBench benchmark datasets. Table cite119†2 presents the ASR scores accross three distinct setups: (a) base, (b) $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ that doesn’t incorporate default system prompts, and lastly (c) $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$, which includes the default system prompts. The variant base doesn’t includes SABER. In overall assessment, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ performs better than other variations i.e.
L271: base and $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$. While $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ achieves an ASR score of $91.0$ and $83.0$ for L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh on JbBench, that corresponds to relative gains of $27\%$ and $50\%$ against $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$, respectively, the variant base scores only $0.0$ and $2.0$. The pattern in the PPL scores for the remaining sets indicate a consistent performance for the first two models, i.e. L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh, but a fluctuation in NoENorm for the remaining ones.

L290: ## 7 Discussion
L291: ### 7.1 Comparative Analysis
L292: Table cite118†1 demonstrates a consistent advantage of SABER over the baselines across all evaluated models on HarmBench (c.f. Table cite118†1 ). The strongest baseline $\text{GCG}^{{\ddagger}}$ achieves ASR scores of $34.5$, $28.0$, $90.0$ and $88.0$ for L2-7BCh, L2-13BCh, V-7B and M-7BInstV2, respectively. However, both the variants of SABER, i.e., $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ and $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$, surpass $\text{GCG}^{{\ddagger}}$ in all scenarios.
L293: While the gain of $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ ranges from a minimum of $3.1\%$ to a maximum of $51\%$, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$ achieves at least $3.7\%$ and at most $27.5\%$. Even when comparing the performance of $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ and $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ consistently outperforms $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$, achieving a $22.6\%$ improvement in L2-7BCh and an $18.3\%$ improvement in L2-13BCh.
L294: For V-7B, both variant exhibits comparable performance with a marginal difference of $0.6\%$. A similar outcome is reflected in Table cite119†2 , where $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ demonstrates equivalent or superior performance compared to $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$ for most of the cases. On the JbBench benchmark, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ achieves performance improvements of $27\%$ and $50\%$ over L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh, respectively.
L295: In case of AdvBench, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ yields even greater improvements of $33.9\%$ and $74\%$ over L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh, respectively. These findings highlight the overall superior performance of SABER.

L290: ## 7 Discussion
L291: ### 7.1 Comparative Analysis
L292: Table cite118†1 demonstrates a consistent advantage of SABER over the baselines across all evaluated models on HarmBench (c.f. Table cite118†1 ). The strongest baseline $\text{GCG}^{{\ddagger}}$ achieves ASR scores of $34.5$, $28.0$, $90.0$ and $88.0$ for L2-7BCh, L2-13BCh, V-7B and M-7BInstV2, respectively. However, both the variants of SABER, i.e., $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ and $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$, surpass $\text{GCG}^{{\ddagger}}$ in all scenarios.
L293: While the gain of $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ ranges from a minimum of $3.1\%$ to a maximum of $51\%$, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$ achieves at least $3.7\%$ and at most $27.5\%$. Even when comparing the performance of $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ and $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ consistently outperforms $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$, achieving a $22.6\%$ improvement in L2-7BCh and an $18.3\%$ improvement in L2-13BCh.
L294: For V-7B, both variant exhibits comparable performance with a marginal difference of $0.6\%$. A similar outcome is reflected in Table cite119†2 , where $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ demonstrates equivalent or superior performance compared to $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}$ for most of the cases. On the JbBench benchmark, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ achieves performance improvements of $27\%$ and $50\%$ over L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh, respectively.
L295: In case of AdvBench, $\texttt{SABER}^{{\dagger}}$ yields even greater improvements of $33.9\%$ and $74\%$ over L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh, respectively. These findings highlight the overall superior performance of SABER.
L296: ### 7.2 Insights into Variational Differences of SABER
L297: We observe a trade-off between PPL and ASR considering each variation across all models. SABER yields the highest average ASR ($93.9\%$) with only a marginal increase in average PPL ($7.4$ in comparison to $7.3$ in Org). Interestingly, NoLNorm is comparable to SABER. NoLNorm achieves $90.9\%$ ASR along with the lowest average PPL of $7.3$. The last variation IntP also scores a noticeable ASR ($88.4\%$) with a modest increase in PPL (from $7.3$ to $7.8$).
L298: In contrast to other variations, NoENorm performs worst with an average ASR of 31.1 and an average PPL of $37.2$. Note that NoLNorm does not use the layer-normalized $\tilde{h}_{i}^{s}$ but leverages the Euclidean norm on $h_{i}^{s}$; yet achieves performance comparable to SABER. Interestingly, the variant NoENorm uses the layer-normalized $\tilde{h}_{i}^{s}$ but skips Euclidean norm, which leads to the weakest performance among all variants. It highlights the importance of Euclidean Norm in SABER.
L299: ### 7.3 Critical Insights into SABER
L300: 
L301: cite121†Image: Refer to caption Figure 3: An illustration of the impact of skipping layers on model behavior for L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh (excludes SABER): As more layers are skipped, the denial rates (dotted lines) for harmful inputs decrease but the hallucination rates (solid lines) increase in both models.
L302: To comprehend the influence of cross-layer residual connections on the underlying models, we conduct a study in which we systematically skip layers as opposed to use them in a residual connection. For each validation instance in $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$, we randomly skip $n$ layers^{13}^{13} 13 The value of $n$ ranges from $1$ to $7$. from the identified region mentioned in Algorithm cite101†1 .
L303: We classify the responses into three categories using Llama-3-70B-Instruct: (a) Success: if the model entertains the harmful inputs, (b) Denial: when the model refuses to answer, and (c) Hallucination: if the model produces irrelevant output. We opt for L2-7BCh and L2-13BCh due to their substantial gain in ASR scores when augmented with SABER. Figure cite122†3 highlights a pronounced inverse relationship between denial and hallucination.
L304: For both of the models, hallucination rates spike while denial rates drop as the number of skipped layers increase. This trade-off explains why SABER is effective for a successful jailbreak. SABER creates an alternative pathway rather completely avoiding layers that preserves the original computation. It helps to maintain coherency and prevents hallucinations, while the residual pathway reduces the likelihood of denial responses.
L305: By carefully calibrating the strength of the residual connection with the optimal scaling factor $\lambda^{*}$, SABER achieves an optimal balance in reducing denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations. Additional details about the analysis is given in Appendix cite42†B .

L340: Note that the scaling factor $\lambda$ introduces a trade-off between attack effectiveness and preservation of the model’s original capabilities. Increasing $\lambda$ improves attack success rates. The root cause of the degradation may lie in the mechanism of SABER. It introduces a scaled residual signal into the model’s internal representations, guided by the triplet of parameters $(s^{*},e^{*},\lambda^{*})$. $\lambda$ controls the magnitude of the injected signal.
L341: As $\lambda$ increases, the perturbation becomes more prominent during the forward pass. It steers the internal computation toward the desired output. Consequently, the attack achieves higher success rates, as demonstrated in our results (c.f. Table cite118†1 and cite119†2 ). However, this approach comes with a cost i.e. an interfere with the computations that underlie the model’s general-purpose language understanding and reasoning abilities.
L342: ## 9 Conclusion
L343: In this paper, we introduced a novel approach, SABER that incorporates an additional residual connection between two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$. SABER creates a controlled pathway that systematically reduces the likelihood of denial responses. Our experiments demonstrated that Euclidean norm-based scaling plays a pivotal role in SABER and contributes significantly to its superior performance.
L344: We observed that SABER effectively preserves its language modeling capabilities while achieving the highest ASR performance, highlighting its dual efficacy in both language comprehension and evasion tasks. These observations collectively highlight a critical vulnerability: open-source language models are vulnerable to subtle architectural perturbations.
L345: ## 10 Limitation
L346: Despite the promising performance of SABER, it still has space for further development and exploration. First, the cross-layer residual connection connects layer $s^{*}$ to layer $e^{*}$. However, the outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored. Second, we compute the optimal value of $\lambda$ from a predefined set of candidate values; Nonetheless, the optimal value of $\lambda$ in a continuous space is yet to be studied. SABER exhibits a certain limitation in reasoning capability.
L347: Although language comprehension and generation capabilities in LLMs remain intact (c.f. Section cite24†6.3 ), there is a notable adverse impact on reasoning ability (c.f. Appendix cite29†8 ) when SABER is employed. Finally, our study includes models ranging from $7$B to $13$B in size. The influence of SABER on larger models remains an open question.
L348: ## 11 Ethical Considerations
L349: We honestly present the findings of our research work while maintaining transparency throughout the entire process. This research work uses the publicly available datasets-HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench. For the underlying models, it employes Llama-2-7b-chat, Llama-2-13b-chat, Vicuna-7b, and Mistral-7B-Inst. Lastly, we utilize publicly available frameworks- HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and Language Model Evaluation Harness for evaluation.
L350: Although the purpose of our research is to find vulnerabilities in LLMs, we acknowledge that the findings could be misused for harmful purposes. In such cases, human intervention is required to prevent misuse.
